blocks.label: A  ·  BIG IDEAS
items: 1. List the four units of geologic time, from largest to smallest. Eon, era, period, epoch.
2. In what kind of rock are most fossils found? Why there? Sedimentary rock: layers of sediment bury and preserve the remains.
3. What made oxygen build up in the air (the Great Oxidation Event)? Photosynthesis released oxygen faster than rocks and iron could absorb it (about 2.4 billion years ago).
4. When volcanoes add CO₂ and other greenhouse gases to the air, what happens to temperatures? They go up: Earth warms.
5. When ice sheets grow, what happens to sea level? It falls. When the climate warms again, sea level recovers.
6. What kind of event ends both the Paleozoic Era and the Mesozoic Era? A mass extinction (end-Permian, about 252 million years ago; K–Pg, about 66 million years ago).
7. Since the age of the dinosaurs, has Earth's climate warmed or cooled? Cooled, gradually, as the Mesozoic greenhouse faded, ending in repeated ice ages.

blocks.label: B  ·  THE PRECAMBRIAN
items: Eons Name the three, oldest to youngest: Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic.
Time About how much of Earth's history does it cover? About 88%.
Hadean What was happening to the young Earth? Earth forms (about 4.54 billion years ago); dense iron sinks to form the core.
Archean What formed on the surface? What lived there? Long-lasting crust and oceans; microbes (microbial ecosystems).
Proterozoic How did the air change? Why did it matter for life? Oxygen rose (Great Oxidation Event). That made complex, oxygen-using life possible: eukaryotes, then multicellular life.
What was Snowball Earth, and when did it happen? Ice spread over nearly all of Earth, even near the equator: the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations, about 720–635 million years ago (Proterozoic).
The thaw What ended Snowball Earth? Volcanoes kept releasing CO₂. It built up until Earth warmed enough to melt the ice.

blocks.label: C–E  ·  PERIOD BY PERIOD
rows: Cambrian
Shallow seas; their sand, mud and lime became sandstone, shale and limestone.
Only in the sea: life was entirely marine.
Greenhouse (warm), high sea levels, less oxygen than today.
Animal body plans diversified rapidly (trilobites, mollusks, sponges), starting about 539 million years ago, over tens of millions of years.
Ordovician
Shallow seas; plate collisions started new mountain building.
Reefs and jawless fishes; early land plants.
It cooled; ice grew and sea level fell. Major extinctions followed.
Silurian
Laurentia and Baltica (Caledonian mountain building).
Jawed fishes; small vascular plants and land arthropods built the first land communities.
It warmed, and sea levels recovered.
Devonian
In warm, shallow seas; continental collisions continued.
Forests, insects and early tetrapods (four-limbed animals).
Warm and shallow, until late-Devonian crises; extinctions hit hard.
Fish diversified hugely: armored placoderms, early sharks, lobe-finned fish.
Carboniferous
Pangaea, through major collisions (the Appalachians kept growing).
Giant arthropods (Meganeura, Arthropleura) and amphibians; the amniotic egg let reptiles reproduce away from water.
Oxygen rose above modern levels as CO₂ fell; the tropics stayed warm while southern Gondwana glaciated.
Coal: thick plant material buried in tropical swamps (wetlands) later became coal.
Permian
Pangaea, fully assembled; one ocean, Panthalassa; a dry interior.
No. It was a synapsid, on the mammal line.
Severe warming and widespread ocean oxygen loss.
Siberian Traps volcanism released greenhouse gases: warming and ocean oxygen loss. Most marine species died, about 252 million years ago.
Triassic
Late-Triassic rifting began to break it apart.
Ecosystems rebuilt, over millions of years; reptiles diversified.
Hot, dry and strongly seasonal.
The first dinosaurs, about 230 million years ago (not yet dominant).
Jurassic
The Atlantic (and the Gulf of Mexico), as Pangaea split apart.
Giant sauropods (Diplodocus, Brachiosaurus) and theropods (Allosaurus); marine reptiles in the sea, pterosaurs in the air.
Greenhouse; shallow seas covered large areas.
A feathered dinosaur near the origin of birds, about 150 million years ago.
Cretaceous
High seas; Antarctica even had forests.
Flowering plants; dinosaurs flourished, and small mammals were present.
Greenhouse, with high sea levels.
A 10 km asteroid hit near the Yucatán (Chicxulub), about 66 million years ago; about 75% of species died, including all non-bird dinosaurs.
Paleogene
India, which began building the Himalaya.
Mammals, which diversified rapidly.
Gradual cooling, as the Mesozoic greenhouse faded.
Neogene
The Himalaya and the Andes.
Grasslands; grazing mammals diversified with them.
Cooler and drier.
Quaternary
Continental ice sheets, several kilometers thick.
Humans (modern mammals and birds diversified).
Milankovitch cycles: changes in Earth's orbit and tilt.
The warm interglacial we live in now (the last 11,700 years).
